```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Run API-backed examples only when an IUCN API key is available.
has_iucn_api_key <- nzchar(trimws(Sys.getenv("IUCN_REDLIST_KEY", unset = "")))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#",
  eval = FALSE
)
```

## Setup:

```{r setup, eval = TRUE}
library(redlistManipulatr)
```

## Functions:

### Getting a list of all species on the Red List

`RL_sp_list()` retrieves the latest global assessment summary from the current kingdom-level endpoints in `rredlist`. The summary includes the SIS taxon ID, scientific name, Kingdom, and assessment category. The current endpoint does not provide the other taxonomic ranks or population information available from the retired endpoint.

The function reads the API key by default from `Sys.getenv("IUCN_REDLIST_KEY")`. Set `IUCN_REDLIST_KEY=your.api.key` in your `.Renviron` file, or pass `key` explicitly. API keys are available through the account page at <https://api.iucnredlist.org/>.

The `retain.category` parameter controls whether the assessment category is included. `retain.population` is retained for compatibility, but the current summary endpoint does not provide population information; requesting it produces a warning. Use `RL_population()` with assessment IDs to retrieve structured population fields from full assessment records.

`retain.taxonomic.info` controls which available taxonomic fields are retained: all available fields (`"all"`), Kingdom and Class when supplied (`"some"`), or none (`"none"`). The current summary endpoint supplies Kingdom only. The taxon ID and scientific name are always returned.

``` {r, eval = FALSE}

sp_list <-
  RL_sp_list(
    retain.taxonomic.info = "some",
    retain.population = FALSE,
    retain.category = TRUE
  )

```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}
sp_list <-
  RL_sp_list(
    retain.taxonomic.info = "some",
    retain.population = FALSE,
    retain.category = TRUE
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(sp_list[1:10,])

```

### Getting population information for selected assessments

`RL_population()` retrieves structured population fields from full assessment records. It requires assessment IDs; the SIS taxon IDs in the `taxonid` column returned by `RL_sp_list()` are a different identifier. Set `include.documentation = TRUE` to include the population narrative when it is available. See `?RL_population()` for the returned fields.

### Obtaining habitat and elevation data from the Red List

`RL_fetch()` obtains habitat and elevation data from the Red List API.

Supply species names or IUCN Red List IDs through `x`, as a vector, list, or `data.frame`. Set `query` to `"name"` or `"ID"` to choose the lookup type. If `x` is a `data.frame`, use `col.name` to identify the column containing the names or IDs.

The function reads the API key by default from `Sys.getenv("IUCN_REDLIST_KEY")`. Set `IUCN_REDLIST_KEY=your.api.key` in your `.Renviron` file, or pass `key` explicitly. API keys are available through the account page at <https://api.iucnredlist.org/>.

A simple example could look like:

``` {r, eval = FALSE}
# Fetch data from the Red List:
df <- 
  RL_fetch(
    x = 
      c(
        "Panthera leo", 
        "Parus major",
        "Pinus oocarpa"
      ),
    query = "name"
  )
```
``` {r, echo = FALSE, eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

df <- 
  RL_fetch(
    x = 
      c(
        "Panthera leo", 
        "Parus major",
        "Pinus oocarpa"
      ),
    query = "name"
  )

```

This returns a `data.frame` in wide format. The table below shows only some columns.

Habitat suitability codes include `3` for Suitable, `2` for Marginal, and `5` for Unknown; missing suitability is coded as `999`. See the `suitability` dataset.

Habitat major importance is coded as `1` for Yes, `2` for No, and `3` for missing values. See the `major_importance` dataset.

The suitability and major-importance codes are concatenated in each habitat cell. For example, `31` represents suitable habitat of major importance.

If a species has no habitat data, its habitat columns contain `66`.

If elevation data are missing, minimum and maximum elevation are set to `-99999` and `99999`, respectively.
Season codes follow the Red List: `1` is Resident, `2` is Breeding Season, `3` is Non-breeding Season, `4` is Passage, and `5` is Seasonal Occurrence Uncertain. Missing season codes are represented by `999`. See the `seasons` dataset.

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df[,1:18])

```

`RL_fetch()` also allows for additional customisation. 

By default it runs in parallel, but this can be altered by setting the parameter `parallel` to `FALSE`. If running in parallel, the number of cores can also be specified manually using `num.cores`.

It can also be tested on a subset of data, set by changing `subset` to the proportion of data desired. 

The duration of sleep between each call to the Red List API can also be manually set using `sleep_dur`.

Finally, there are 3 options for `verbose`. `verbose = 0` gives no progress update, `verbose = 1` gives a progress bar (the default), and `verbose = 2` prints one line for each task completed.

For more details see `?RL_fetch()`.

### Recoding Level 1 or Level 2 habitats

`RL_code_fill()` copies values from Level 2 categories to their Level 1 parent, or from a Level 1 category to its Level 2 categories. The `level1.recode` and `level2.recode` parameters control these directions.

It takes a wide-format `data.frame` such as the output of `RL_fetch()`.

Run `RL_code_fill()` once on a dataset. Repeated calls can propagate values added by earlier calls.

Example use:

``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
df2 <-
  RL_code_fill(
    x = df,
    level1.recode = TRUE,
    level2.recode = FALSE
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df2[,1:18])

```

Additional parameters `subset`, `parallel`, `num.cores`, and `verbose` operate the same as for `RL_fetch()`.

See `?RL_code_fill()` for more details.

### Recoding missing habitat suitabilities and seasons

Some species have seasonal occurrence for a particular habitat missing on the Red List, or else have habitat suitability missing. In these cases, `RL_fetch()` pulls down this data as `999`. This behaviour may not be desired, and the functions `RL_recode_seasons()` and `RL_recode_suitabilities()` exist to recode these values.

`RL_recode_suitabilities()` recodes `999` habitat suitabilities as 'Suitable', giving a code of `3` (see the `suitability` data).

`RL_recode_seasons()` recodes `999` seasons as 'Resident', giving a code of `1` (see the `seasons` data).

Recoding seasons can create duplicate Resident rows when both Resident and missing-season data are present. Set `combine.rows = TRUE` to combine these rows, retaining the highest-ranked suitability-major importance value for each habitat according to `suitability_ordered`. If both recoding functions are needed, run `RL_recode_suitabilities()` first so missing suitability values are replaced before rows are combined. `combine.rows` defaults to `FALSE`.

`combine.rows = FALSE`: 

``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
df3 <-
  RL_recode_seasons(
    x = df2,
    combine.rows = FALSE
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df3[,1:18])

```

`combine.rows = TRUE`: 
``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
df3 <-
  RL_recode_seasons(
    x = df2,
    combine.rows = TRUE
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df3[,1:18])

```

See `?RL_recode_suitabilities()` or `?RL_recode_seasons()` for more details.

### Checking elevation values

An assessment can contain a minimum elevation greater than its maximum elevation. `RL_elevation_check()` finds these rows and replaces the minimum and maximum values with `-99999` and `99999`, respectively, by default.

It accepts a wide- or long-format `data.frame`, including data from `RL_reformat_long()`.

See `?RL_elevation_check()` for more details and other options.

### Subsetting to desired seasons

In some cases, a species may have particular seasons which are desired and others which are not. `RL_subset_seasons()` allows you to subset to the seasons you'd like to have data for.

Once again, `x` is a wide format `data.frame` as output by `RL_fetch()` or any function manipulating it.

`season_df` is a `data.frame` with at least two columns: one for species names or IDs and one for desired season codes. Include one row per desired species-season combination. By default, the first two columns are used; set `species.col.name` and `season.col.name` to choose different columns. Set `query` to `"name"` or `"ID"` to match the identifiers in `x`.

`RL_subset_seasons()` can also fill a desired season that is absent from the data. For example, if Resident is desired but only Breeding Season and Non-breeding Season records are available, set `fill.missing.seasons = c(2, 3)` to allow those records to supply values. For each habitat, the highest-ranked suitability-major importance value is selected according to `suitability_ordered`.

Set `retain.na.seasons = TRUE` to retain missing seasons (coded as `999` by `RL_fetch()`) even when they are not listed in `season_df`. The default is `FALSE`; another option is to recode them first with `RL_recode_seasons()`.

Set `retain.missing.sp = TRUE` to retain species in `x` that are absent from `season_df`. Species listed in `season_df` are still subset to the requested seasons. This option defaults to `TRUE`.

``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
my_seasons <-
  data.frame(
    species = c("Panthera leo",
                "Pinus oocarpa"),
    seasons = 1
  )

df4 <-
     RL_subset_seasons(
         x = df2,
         season_df = my_seasons,
         query = "name",
         fill.missing.seasons = c(2, 3),
         retain.na.seasons = FALSE,
         retain.missing.sp = FALSE
     )

```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

rownames(df4) <- 1:nrow(df4)

knitr::kable(df4[,1:18])

```

See `RL_subset_seasons()` for more details.

### Subsetting to retain only some habitat suitabilities or major importances

For Area of Habitat (AOH) maps or similar analyses, you may want to retain only selected habitat suitability or major-importance values. `RL_subset_acceptable()` lets you choose which codes to keep; other values are replaced with `NA`.

`acceptable_suitabilities` and `acceptable_importances` each take a vector input of suitability/major importance codes (see the `suitability` and `major_importance` datasets) of which to retain. Both default to accepting all, meaning that specifying `acceptable_suitabilities` without specifying `acceptable_importances` will only filter by suitability.

`na.rm` allows you to specify whether a row should be removed if all of its habitat classes are changed to `NA`. This defaults to `TRUE`.

``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}

df5 <-
  RL_subset_acceptable(
    x = df4,
    acceptable_suitabilities = c(3, 999),
    acceptable_importances = 1
  )

```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df5[,1:18])

```

See `?RL_subset_acceptable()` for more details.

### Crosswalking habitat classes to a look-up table

You can map Red List habitat classes to another classification, such as land cover, using a look-up table. `RL_crosswalk()` supports one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many mappings from `lut` applied to a wide-format input `x`.

The default `lut`, `hab_conversion_lut`, maps habitat classes to integer column names; for example, `1.1` maps to `110` and `9.8.1` maps to `981`.

If supplying your own `lut`, the parameters `new.code.colname` and `old.code.colname` allow you to specify which columns of `lut` correspond to the new values and the old IUCN habitat codes. This defaults to the first column for new values and the second for old values if these parameters are not specified.

Use `recode` to choose how habitat values are handled. `"no"` retains the existing suitability-major importance code, choosing the highest-ranked value from `suitability_ordered` when several old classes map to one new class. `"one"` assigns `1` to each non-missing value, and `"colname"` assigns the new habitat column name.

If only selected suitability or major-importance values should be retained, apply `RL_subset_acceptable()` before `RL_crosswalk()`.


``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
df6 <-
  RL_crosswalk(
    x = df5,
    recode = "colname"
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df6[,1:18])

```
See `?RL_crosswalk()` for more details.

### Reformatting to other formats

So far, the examples have used wide-format data (one column per habitat category). Long-format data (one row per species-season-habitat combination) can be useful for other analyses.

`RL_reformat_long()` converts wide data to long format and can be used before crosswalking with `RL_crosswalk()`. The `x` argument is the input `data.frame`; `na.rm` controls whether rows with missing or no habitat information are removed. It defaults to `TRUE`.

``` {r, eval = has_iucn_api_key}
df7 <-
  RL_reformat_long(
    x = df5,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
```

``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df7[,])

```

`RL_reformat_wide()` converts the output of `RL_reformat_long()` back to wide format. Supply the long-format `data.frame` through `x`.

### Obtaining threat information from the Red List

`RL_threats()` retrieves threat information from the Red List API and returns one row per species-threat combination.

As with `RL_fetch()`, supply species names or IUCN Red List IDs through `x` as a vector, list, or `data.frame`. Set `query` to `"name"` or `"ID"`. For a `data.frame`, use `col.name` to identify the column containing the names or IDs.

The function reads the API key by default from `Sys.getenv("IUCN_REDLIST_KEY")`. Set `IUCN_REDLIST_KEY=your.api.key` in your `.Renviron` file, or pass `key` explicitly. API keys are available through the account page at <https://api.iucnredlist.org/>.

A simple example could look like:

``` {r, eval = FALSE}
# Fetch data from the Red List:
df8 <- 
  RL_threats(
    x = 
      c(
        "Panthera leo"
      ),
    query = "name"
  )
```
``` {r, echo = FALSE, eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

df8 <- 
  RL_threats(
    x = 
      c(
        "Panthera leo"
      ),
    query = "name"
  )

```
``` {r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_iucn_api_key, include = has_iucn_api_key}

knitr::kable(df8)

```

`RL_threats()` also allows for additional customisation. 

By default it runs in parallel, but this can be altered by setting the parameter `parallel` to `FALSE`. If running in parallel, the number of cores can also be specified manually using `num.cores`.

It can also be tested on a subset of data, set by changing `subset` to the proportion of data desired. 

The duration of sleep between each call to the Red List API can also be manually set using `sleep_dur`.

Finally, there are 3 options for `verbose`. `verbose = 0` gives no progress update, `verbose = 1` gives a progress bar (the default), and `verbose = 2` prints one line for each task completed.

For more details see `?RL_threats()`.

### Exporting

Export a result as a CSV file with:

``` {r, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(
  df7,
  file = "path/to/directory/file.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

```
